author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the structural components of DNA — the sugar-phosphate backbone, the four nitrogenous bases, and the hydrogen bonds between base pairs — and describe how they assemble into the double helix.
Apply the complementary base-pairing rules (A with T, G with C) to determine one strand's sequence from its complement, and explain why A-T forms two hydrogen bonds and G-C forms three.
Describe the antiparallel orientation of the two DNA strands and explain how the 5'-to-3' directionality of each backbone determines this arrangement.
Trace the action of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork, identifying each enzyme's function.

Explain why replication yields a continuous leading strand and a discontinuous lagging strand of Okazaki fragments, relating this to the unidirectional 5'-to-3' activity of DNA polymerase on antiparallel templates.
Articulate why DNA replication is semiconservative and predict the composition of daughter molecules after one and two rounds of replication.

modules.description: A flat, schematic ladder representation of DNA introduces the sugar-phosphate backbones, the four color-coded bases, and base pairing before any 3D complexity.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recognize the two sugar-phosphate backbones as the sides of the DNA ladder.
Identify the four nitrogenous bases by one-letter abbreviation and color code.
Understand that bases project inward and pair across the ladder with their complements.

components.text:
A = adenine (red)   T = thymine (blue)
G = guanine (yellow)   C = cytosine (green)

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the DNA ladder schematic and title so students see the overall repeating structure first.
clips.narration: Welcome. DNA is a polymer with a strikingly regular structure. Here it is drawn as a ladder: the two vertical sides are the sugar-phosphate backbones, and the rungs between them are pairs of nitrogenous bases.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal backbone labels on both sides to name the structural sides of the ladder.
clips.narration: Each side is a repeating chain of sugars and phosphates. This backbone is chemically identical up and down its length, giving DNA its uniform, repeating scaffold.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the color/letter legend for the four bases and briefly pulse the ladder to draw attention to the rungs.
clips.narration: The rungs are made of two colored halves that meet in the middle. Adenine is red, thymine blue, guanine yellow, cytosine green. Notice the bases always project inward to pair with a complement on the opposite strand.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2 — From Ladder to Double Helix
modules.description: The schematic ladder twists into the realistic double helix. Students toggle between representations and observe the helical geometry and its grooves.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Map the schematic ladder onto the realistic double-helix geometry.
Observe that the backbones spiral around a common axis with bases stacked inside.
Recognize that the helix completes roughly one full turn every ten base pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: Start with the familiar ladder on the left so students anchor to the prior scene before transformation.
clips.narration: We start again from the ladder you just met. This flat schematic is easy to read, but it is not what DNA actually looks like inside a cell.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal the rotating realistic helix beside the ladder to build the mental mapping between the two representations.
clips.narration: Now watch the same molecule twist. The backbones spiral around a common axis and the base pairs stack along the interior, forming the famous double helix.

clips.changeMeaning: Add the ten-base-pair turn note and grow the helix slightly to emphasize the periodicity and grooves.
clips.narration: The helix completes roughly one full turn every ten base pairs. You can also see grooves winding along its surface — simply features of this geometry. Toggle between the ladder and helix any time to keep both pictures in mind.

modules.description: The helix is shown with directional arrows and 5'/3' end labels, emphasizing the antiparallel arrangement forced by backbone chemistry.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the 5' and 3' termini at the ends of each backbone.
Describe the antiparallel orientation of the two strands.
Explain that antiparallel arrangement is forced by the directional chemistry of the backbone.

clips.changeMeaning: Present a rotatable helix so students can inspect direction from any angle before labels appear.
clips.narration: This is the realistic helix again. Grab and rotate it — we are about to give each strand a direction.

clips.changeMeaning: Add the two oppositely pointing directional arrows to visualize antiparallel orientation.
clips.narration: Here are arrows along each backbone. One strand's arrow points up; the other points down. The two strands always run in opposite directions — they are antiparallel.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal 5' and 3' end labels on both strands, connecting directionality to the sugar carbons.
clips.narration: The ends are labeled 5' and 3', named for carbon atoms of the sugar ring. Where one strand reads 5' to 3' downward, its partner reads 5' to 3' upward. This arrangement is not optional — the directional chemistry of the backbone forces it.

modules.description: Students complete a complementary strand by dragging bases onto an empty backbone; correct pairs snap in and form hydrogen bonds (two for A-T, three for G-C).
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply complementary base-pairing rules to build a complementary strand.
Relate hydrogen-bond count to base-pair identity and strength.
Recognize the new strand runs antiparallel (3'-to-5') to the template.

components.scriptDescription: Manages an interactive complementary base-pairing puzzle. Holds a template sequence (default 5'-ATGCCAGT-3') displayed on the left half-ladder, and a list of empty rung slots on the right backbone. Exposes public references to the loose base objects (adeninePalette, thyminePalette, guaninePalette, cytosinePalette) and to a hydrogenBond visual prefab. When a base object is dropped near a slot, it checks the complementary rule (A pairs with T, G pairs with C): on a correct match it snaps the base into the slot and instantiates the correct number of dashed hydrogen-bond lines (2 for A-T, 3 for G-C); on an incorrect match it rejects the base, returns it to the palette, and fires a public UnityEvent onIncorrect with an explanation string. Fires onComplete when all slots are filled. Inputs: sequence string, slot count, references to palette bases and bond prefab. Outputs: onCorrect, onIncorrect, onComplete UnityEvents.

components.text: Complete the strand: drag bases to pair with 5'-ATGCCAGT-3'

clips.changeMeaning: Present the template strand and base palette so students can start the interactive pairing task.
clips.narration: Here is one complete strand, 5'-ATGCCAGT-3', and an empty backbone beside it. Below is a palette of loose bases. Drag each base up to pair correctly with the template.

components.text: A–T = 2 hydrogen bonds   •   G–C = 3 hydrogen bonds

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasize hydrogen-bond feedback rules by highlighting the prompt as students place bases.
clips.narration: Correct pairs snap in and form hydrogen bonds — two dashed lines for A with T, three for G with C. An incorrect pairing is rejected with a short explanation. Those extra bonds make G-C pairs stronger.

clips.changeMeaning: Confirm the completed complementary sequence and its antiparallel 3'-to-5' direction after the puzzle is solved.
clips.narration: Well done. The complementary strand reads 3'-TACGGTCA-5' — running in the opposite direction to the template, exactly the antiparallel arrangement we saw earlier.

modules.description: A section of realistic helix is unwound by helicase, which moves along the DNA breaking hydrogen bonds and separating the strands at the replication fork.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify helicase as the enzyme that opens the double helix.
Describe that helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between paired bases.
Recognize the replication fork as the site where strands separate.

components.scriptDescription: Moves an enzyme object along a straight replication-fork path at a configurable speed. Inputs: startPosition (Vector3), endPosition (Vector3), travelSeconds (float), and an optional target DNA object reference. As the object travels from start to end over travelSeconds, it drives a normalized progress value 0..1 that other components can read via a public property CurrentProgress, and exposes a public UnityEvent onReachEnd fired when it arrives. Loops or stops based on a public loop bool. Used to make helicase, polymerase, and ligase crawl along the DNA.

clips.changeMeaning: Show a fresh intact section of double helix to set the stage for replication.
clips.narration: To replicate, the cell must first open the double helix. Here is a fresh stretch of DNA, still fully wound.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce helicase at one end of the helix as the first replication enzyme.
clips.narration: The first enzyme is helicase. It docks at one end of the helix, ready to pry the two strands apart.

clips.changeMeaning: Move helicase along the DNA to unwind the strands, showing hydrogen bonds breaking behind it.
clips.narration: Watch helicase travel along the DNA. It breaks the hydrogen bonds between paired bases, unzipping the helix and exposing each strand as a template for replication.

modules.description: As helicase separates the strands, single-strand binding proteins attach to the exposed strands to keep them open and stable.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify single-strand binding proteins (SSBs) and their location on exposed strands.
Explain that SSBs stabilize single-stranded DNA and prevent re-pairing.
Recognize why open, accessible strands are required for replication.

clips.changeMeaning: Resume from where helicase left off, with the strands separated but no stabilizing proteins yet.
clips.narration: We resume just behind helicase. The strands are now separated — but single-stranded DNA is unstable and tends to snap back together or fold on itself.

clips.changeMeaning: Attach single-strand binding proteins to the exposed strands to stabilize them.
clips.narration: To prevent that, single-strand binding proteins latch onto the exposed strands, coating them so they stay open and accessible.

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasize the stabilizing role by noting collapse would occur without SSBs, reinforcing their function.
clips.narration: Without these proteins, the strands would collapse back together and replication could not proceed. The SSBs hold the template strands ready for the machinery that comes next.

modules.moduleName: Scene 7 — DNA Polymerase & the Leading Strand
modules.description: DNA polymerase synthesizes the leading strand continuously, following the fork, adding nucleotides only to the 3' end (building 5' to 3').
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify DNA polymerase and its 5'-to-3' synthesis direction.
Explain that the leading strand is synthesized continuously toward the fork.
Recognize that polymerase requires a primer to begin extension.

components.scriptDescription: Moves an enzyme object along a straight replication-fork path at a configurable speed. Inputs: startPosition (Vector3), endPosition (Vector3), travelSeconds (float), and an optional target DNA object. Drives a normalized CurrentProgress 0..1 during travel and fires onReachEnd when finished. A public loop bool controls looping. Here it carries polymerase continuously along the leading-strand template toward the fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the open template with polymerase placed on the leading-strand template.
clips.narration: Now DNA polymerase arrives. It settles on the template strand that lets synthesis run in the same direction the fork is moving.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce free nucleotides pairing with the template as polymerase builds the new strand.
clips.narration: Free nucleotides drift in from solution, pair with the template, and are added to the growing new strand. Polymerase can only add to the 3' end, so it builds strictly 5' to 3' — and it needs a short primer to start.

clips.changeMeaning: Move polymerase continuously toward the fork to show the leading strand growing without interruption.
clips.narration: On this template, polymerase moves continuously, chasing the fork and laying down one unbroken complementary strand. This is the leading strand.

modules.description: On the opposite template, synthesis is discontinuous: polymerase makes short Okazaki fragments moving away from the fork, later joined by DNA ligase.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why the lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously.
Identify Okazaki fragments and the direction of their synthesis.
Identify DNA ligase as the enzyme that joins fragments into a continuous strand.

components.scriptDescription: Moves an enzyme object along a straight path at a configurable speed. Inputs: startPosition, endPosition, travelSeconds, optional target object. Drives normalized CurrentProgress 0..1 and fires onReachEnd. Here it carries ligase along the lagging strand; other components can read CurrentProgress to visually seal Okazaki fragment junctions as ligase passes over them.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the other template with polymerase forced to work away from the fork, framing the discontinuity problem.
clips.narration: The other template runs the opposite way. Its 3' end points away from the fork, so polymerase cannot simply chase the fork — it is forced to work backward, away from it.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal a series of Okazaki fragments to show discontinuous synthesis in repeated short pieces.
clips.narration: So the strand is built in short pieces called Okazaki fragments. Polymerase makes one fragment, jumps back toward the fork, and starts another — again and again.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce DNA ligase moving along and sealing fragment junctions into a continuous strand.
clips.narration: Finally DNA ligase moves along and seals the junctions between fragments, stitching them into one continuous lagging strand.

modules.description: All five components operate together at the fork. Students rotate the assembly and review each enzyme's function via a summary panel.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify all five replication components and their positions at the fork.
Match each enzyme to its function.
Link the leading/lagging asymmetry to the antiparallel structure of DNA.

components.text:
helicase – unwinds helix
SSBs – stabilize strands
polymerase (leading) – continuous
polymerase (lagging) – fragments
ligase – seals fragments

clips.changeMeaning: Display the full assembled, rotating fork with all components active for holistic viewing.
clips.narration: Here is the whole replication fork in action. Helicase leads at the front, SSBs hold the strands open, one polymerase runs continuously, another works in fragments, and ligase seals behind it. Rotate it and find each component.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal the enzyme summary panel listing each component's function for review.
clips.narration: This panel lists all five players and what each one does — a quick reference as you inspect the fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Tie the leading/lagging asymmetry back to antiparallel structure, delivering the key conceptual link.
clips.narration: Here is the key idea the lab has built toward: because the two template strands are antiparallel and polymerase can only work 5' to 3', the two new strands must be made differently — one continuous, one in fragments. The structure of DNA dictates how it copies itself.

modules.description: A gold parental molecule replicates into gold/silver hybrids; students predict the composition after a second round before it plays out.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why replication is semiconservative.
Predict daughter-molecule composition after one and two rounds of replication.
Connect the outcome to the design logic of the Meselson-Stahl experiment.

components.text:
After a 2nd round, the four molecules are:
A) all half gold, half silver
B) two hybrid, two fully silver
C) all fully silver

components.scriptDescription: Presents a multiple-choice prediction question with three selectable options (A, B, C) rendered as interactable buttons. Inputs: correctOptionIndex (int, here 1 for option B), and references to three button objects and a feedback text field. When the user selects an option, it compares to correctOptionIndex, highlights the chosen button green if correct or red if incorrect, reveals the correct answer, and fires a public UnityEvent onAnswered(bool correct) so the scene can trigger the second-round replication animation. Outputs: onAnswered event and a public bool AnsweredCorrectly.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the gold parental molecule to mark the original strands before replication.
clips.narration: Here is a parental DNA molecule. Both of its strands are gold, marking them as the original material.

clips.changeMeaning: Split into two hybrid daughters with one gold and one silver strand each to demonstrate semiconservation.
clips.narration: After one round of replication, the strands separate and each templates a new silver strand. The result: two daughter molecules, each with one gold strand and one silver strand. Every daughter conserves one original parental strand — that is what semiconservative means.

clips.changeMeaning: Present the prediction quiz asking students to forecast the second-round outcome before it plays.
clips.narration: Now these two hybrids become the starting material for a second round. Before we play it out, predict: what will the four resulting molecules look like? Choose an option.

components.text: Correct: B — two hybrid + two fully silver

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal the correct second-round result of two hybrid and two fully silver molecules and connect to Meselson-Stahl logic.
clips.narration: The answer is B. Each gold strand is conserved in just one molecule, so after round two we have two hybrid molecules and two fully silver ones. This exact prediction is what a famous density experiment confirmed decades ago.

modules.description: A summary screen lists the six concept areas of the lab, highlighting each in turn as narration reviews it.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Review the double-helix structure and base pairing.
Review antiparallel directionality and the replication enzymes.
Review leading/lagging asymmetry and semiconservative replication.

components.text:
1. Double helix: backbones + bases
2. Base pairing: A–T (2 H-bonds), G–C (3)
3. Antiparallel 5'→3' strands
4. Replication enzymes at the fork
5. Leading vs lagging (Okazaki)
6. Semiconservative replication

▶ 2. Base pairing: A–T (2 H-bonds), G–C (3)
3. Antiparallel 5'→3' strands
4. Replication enzymes at the fork

clips.changeMeaning: Display the full recap list and highlight the first two structural concepts as review begins.
clips.narration: Let's review. First, DNA's double helix, built from two sugar-phosphate backbones with bases inside. Second, the base-pairing rules: A with T by two hydrogen bonds, G with C by three.

components.text:
1. Double helix: backbones + bases
2. Base pairing: A–T (2 H-bonds), G–C (3)
▶ 3. Antiparallel 5'→3' strands
▶ 4. Replication enzymes at the fork
5. Leading vs lagging (Okazaki)
6. Semiconservative replication

clips.changeMeaning: Advance the highlight to the antiparallel arrangement and the replication enzymes for continued review.
clips.narration: Third, the two strands run antiparallel, each read 5' to 3' in opposite directions. Fourth, at the fork, helicase unwinds, SSBs stabilize, polymerase synthesizes, and ligase seals.

components.text:
1. Double helix: backbones + bases
2. Base pairing: A–T (2 H-bonds), G–C (3)
3. Antiparallel 5'→3' strands
4. Replication enzymes at the fork
▶ 5. Leading vs lagging (Okazaki)
▶ 6. Semiconservative replication

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the final two concepts (asymmetry and semiconservation) to close the review.
clips.narration: And fifth and sixth: the antiparallel templates force one continuous leading strand and a lagging strand of Okazaki fragments, and because each daughter keeps one parental strand, replication is semiconservative. Nicely done.
